name: Mustard Yellow
lede: Mustard yellow is the deep, slightly warm yellow of the table condiment, a name that grew out of the shorter word mustard.

sections.title: A condiment's color
sections.body:
Dictionaries gloss plain *mustard* as a reddish-yellow and *mustard brown* as a deep brownish-yellow [1]. *Mustard yellow* itself is described as a deep yellow that was popular in the 1930s [1]. The same dictionary's list of yellows includes [[saffron]], nankeen, tarragon and wheat [1].

The name was not always a compliment. In a history of white, Pastoureau lists it with purple as a color a mother would not want on a baby's nurse, calling mustard yellow a dirty color in a discussion of hospital white [2]. That is a European attitude about hygiene, not a fact about the color [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of museum paintings, a color near this swatch turns up in 295 works, 1.24 per cent of the archive [3]. The earliest is a 1326 panel by Simone Martini and the latest a work from 1940, so the tone runs across six centuries of paint [3]. Among painters, Pierre Bonnard stands out with 5 of his works carrying it [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read the numbers as screen colors [3].
